options.explanation: Correct. The notice exists to give the holder an opportunity to object. Had Ashwath Credit signed the intimation in the specified form, the proviso to s. 82(2) would have dispensed with the notice altogether. Silence is treated as no objection.

options.text: Because the intimation was filed after thirty days; if no cause is shown, the Registrar refers the matter to the Central Government under section 87
options.explanation: The notice is not triggered by lateness, and the Registrar makes no reference to the Central Government. Under s. 87 it is the company or a person interested who applies.

options.text: Because the company and the holder disagreed; if no cause is shown, the Registrar decides the dispute and records his finding
options.explanation: The Registrar never adjudicates. If cause IS shown, s. 82(3) requires him only to record a note to that effect in the register and inform the company.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Case: a floating charge, a section 78 filing and a receiver
questions.case: Nirvaan Analytics Limited creates, on 6 October 2026, a charge in favour of Ashwath Credit Limited over 'all computers, servers, software licences and receivables now owned or hereafter acquired'. The company files nothing with the Registrar. Ashwath Credit applies under section 78, and the Registrar gives notice to the company on 16 November 2026. Ashwath Credit pays the fees demanded. The company defaults on the facility, and on 4 January 2027 Ashwath Credit appoints a receiver over the charged assets under a power in the debenture.

readLink.label: Read: Registration by the charge-holder — s. 78 →

questions.stem: The charge created on 6 October 2026 is best described as:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 6 — characteristics of a floating charge

options.text: A fixed charge, because the categories of asset are described in the instrument
options.explanation: Describing a class is not the same as identifying an asset. A fixed charge attaches to specific, ascertained property; here the members of each class change constantly.

options.text: A pledge, because the assets are movable
options.explanation: A pledge requires delivery of possession of the goods to the pledgee. Nirvaan Analytics keeps and uses its computers and collects its own receivables.

options.text: Not a charge at all, because future assets cannot be charged
options.explanation: Future assets can be charged, and a floating charge is the standard device for doing so. Section 85(1) expressly contemplates floating charges.

options.text: A floating charge, because it covers a class of assets present and future that changes in the ordinary course of business, and the company may deal with them until the charge-holder takes a step
options.explanation: Correct. All three of Romer LJ's characteristics are present. The appointment of the receiver on 4 January 2027 will crystallise the charge on to whatever falls within those classes at that moment.

questions.stem: The Registrar gave notice to the company on 16 November 2026 on Ashwath Credit's application. The last date by which the Registrar may allow registration on that application is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 78 — fourteen days after giving notice to the company

options.text: 5 November 2026
options.explanation: That is the expiry of the company's own thirty-day window under s. 77(1), counted from the creation of the charge on 6 October 2026. It is the date that made the section 78 application possible, not the date the Registrar must act by.

options.text: 30 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 78 lets the Registrar allow the registration within fourteen days after giving notice to the company. Fourteen days from 16 November 2026 expires on 30 November 2026 — unless the company registers the charge itself or shows sufficient cause meanwhile.

options.text: 1 December 2026
options.explanation: An off-by-one error, produced by counting the date of the notice itself as day one. The fourteen days run from the day after the notice.

options.text: 16 December 2026
options.explanation: That is thirty days from the notice. Thirty days is the registration and satisfaction period elsewhere in Chapter VI; the Registrar's window under s. 78 is fourteen days.

questions.stem: Ashwath Credit Limited has paid the fees demanded by the Registrar on its section 78 application. It may:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 78, proviso, and s. 86(1)

options.text: Set the fees off against the secured debt only, and not recover them separately
options.explanation: The proviso creates a free-standing entitlement to recover the amount from the company. It is not limited to a set-off against the debt.

options.text: Recover the fees from the officers of the company who were in default
options.explanation: Officers in default are liable to a PENALTY under s. 86(1), which is payable to the State. The proviso to s. 78 makes the fees recoverable from the company, not from its officers.

options.text: Recover from the company the amount of any fees, additional fees or ad valorem fees it paid to the Registrar; and the company remains liable to penalty under section 86(1) notwithstanding that the charge-holder filed
options.explanation: Correct on both limbs. The proviso to s. 78 gives the recovery right, and the opening words of s. 78 register the charge 'without prejudice to' the company's liability for any offence under Chapter VI — the filing by the holder does not cure the company's default.

options.text: Recover the fees from the company, and the company's default is thereby cured so that no penalty is attracted
options.explanation: The recovery right is correct but the cure is not. Section 78 opens with the words 'without prejudice to its liability in respect of any offence under this Chapter'.

questions.stem: On the appointment of the receiver on 4 January 2027, notice of the appointment must be given to the company and the Registrar by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 84(1) and (2)

options.text: Ashwath Credit Limited, being the person who made the appointment under a power contained in the instrument, within thirty days of the appointment
options.explanation: Correct. Section 84(1) puts the duty on the person who obtains the order or makes the appointment. The receiver's own notice duty under s. 84(2) arises only when he CEASES to hold the appointment.

options.text: Nirvaan Analytics Limited, within thirty days of the appointment, since the charge is on its property
options.explanation: The company is the recipient of the notice, not the giver. Section 84(1) names the person who obtained the order or made the appointment.

options.text: The receiver, within thirty days of taking charge of the assets
options.explanation: Two errors. The initial notice is the appointer's duty, and the period runs from the appointment, not from the receiver taking charge.

options.text: Ashwath Credit Limited, within fourteen days of the appointment
options.explanation: The appointer is right but the period is wrong. Fourteen days is the Registrar's window under s. 78 and the show-cause period under s. 82(2); section 84(1) allows thirty days.
